overview.historicalContext:
The quest to solve polynomial equations drove mathematics for centuries. Quadratic equations were solved in antiquity, cubic equations by Cardano (1545), and quartic equations by Ferrari (1545). For 300 years, mathematicians sought a quintic formula. Joseph-Louis Lagrange's 1770 *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique des équations* was the crucial precursor: he analyzed why the classical formulas for degrees 2–4 worked by studying permutations of roots ('resolvents'), and noticed that his method broke down for degree 5 — the resolvent of a quintic had degree 6, not lower.

In parallel, Alexandre-Théophile Vandermonde's *Mémoire sur la résolution des équations* (presented to the Académie in 1770, published in 1771) developed similar resolvent ideas independently and applied them with striking success to the cyclotomic equation $x^{11} - 1 = 0$, exhibiting an explicit radical formula for the eleventh roots of unity. Vandermonde's calculation — which today is recognized as a discrete Fourier transform over $\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z}$ — was the first concrete example of a polynomial of degree above 4 being solved by radicals via group-theoretic considerations. It directly anticipated Gauss's 1801 *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* §VII, where the constructibility of the regular 17-gon was reduced to solving $x^{17} - 1 = 0$ by radicals via the cyclic structure of $(\mathbb{Z}/17\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. Together, Lagrange and Vandermonde isolated the two facts whose tension Galois would resolve fifty years later: resolvents work when the symmetry group has a nice composition series (Vandermonde's success on cyclotomy), and resolvents fail when it does not (Lagrange's degree-6 obstruction for the quintic).

Paolo Ruffini gave an incomplete proof in 1799 that no such formula exists. His 516-page *Teoria generale delle equazioni* attempted to show that no rational function of the roots could serve as a resolvent, but the proof had gaps — notably an incomplete treatment of permutation groups (the concept barely existed). Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who proved key results on permutation groups in 1815 (including that a primitive subgroup of $S_p$ containing a $p$-cycle equals $S_p$), acknowledged Ruffini's priority but did not endorse the proof.

Niels Henrik Abel provided the first rigorous proof in 1824, at age 21. Living in poverty in Norway, Abel could not afford journal publication and self-published a six-page pamphlet (*Mémoire sur les équations algébriques*), compressed to save printing costs, which he sent to leading mathematicians — Gauss reportedly never read it. Abel refined the argument in an 1826 *Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik* paper. He died of tuberculosis in 1829 at age 26, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship in Berlin.

But it was Évariste Galois who revealed the deeper truth: the solvability of a polynomial is determined by the structure of its symmetry group. His theory explains not just why quintics are unsolvable, but precisely which polynomials can be solved by radicals. Galois submitted his work twice to the Académie des Sciences — Cauchy lost or forgot the first manuscript (1829), and Poisson rejected the second (1831) as 'incomprehensible.' Tragically killed in a duel at age 20 in 1832, Galois spent the night before writing a letter to Auguste Chevalier summarizing his theory, with marginal notes including the famous 'je n'ai pas le temps' ('I have not the time').

Galois's manuscripts were finally published by Joseph Liouville in 1846, fourteen years after his death. It took another generation — through the work of Camille Jordan (*Traité des substitutions*, 1870) and others — for the full power of Galois theory to be understood. Today it is fundamental to modern algebra, connecting field extensions to group theory and underpinning algebraic number theory, algebraic geometry, and the Langlands program.
overview.problemStatement:
Theorem (Abel-Ruffini): There is no general solution in radicals to polynomial equations of degree five or higher.

More precisely: there exist polynomials of degree 5 (and higher) whose roots cannot be expressed using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and nth roots applied to the coefficients.

Galois's formulation: A polynomial equation is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.

The symmetric group $S_5$ is not solvable (because the alternating group $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian), so the general quintic, which has Galois group $S_5$, cannot be solved by radicals.

overview.proofStrategy:
The proof connects two seemingly unrelated concepts through Galois's fundamental insight:

1. **FIELD EXTENSIONS**: An element $\alpha \in E$ is *solvable by radicals* over $F$ if it lies in a tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m \ni \alpha$ where each $K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n_i]{a_i})$. Mathlib formalizes this as `IsSolvableByRad F α`.

2. **GALOIS GROUPS**: For a polynomial $q(x) \in F[x]$, its Galois group $\text{Gal}(q) \leq S_n$ captures the symmetries of its roots — the automorphisms of the splitting field that fix $F$. Lean represents this as `q.Gal : Type*`.

3. **THE BRIDGE** (`galois_bridge`): $\alpha \in \text{solvableByRad}(F, E) \Rightarrow \text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_F(\alpha)))$. Each radical step $K_i \to K_{i+1} = K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ yields a cyclic (hence abelian) Galois group quotient; a group built from abelian quotients is solvable.

4. **GROUP THEORY**: A group $G$ is solvable iff its derived series $G \supset [G,G] \supset [[G,G],[G,G]] \supset \cdots$ reaches $\{e\}$. Crucially:
   - $S_2, S_3, S_4$ are solvable (explaining why quadratics, cubics, quartics have radical formulas)
   - $S_5$ is NOT solvable: $D^1(S_5) = A_5$ and $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$, because $A_5$ is perfect ($[A_5, A_5] = A_5$, a consequence of its simplicity)

5. **CONCLUSION** (`not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`): By contrapositive of the bridge, $\neg\,\text{IsSolvable}(\text{Gal}(q)) \Rightarrow \neg\,\text{IsSolvableByRad}\,F\,\alpha$. Since $S_5$ is not solvable and the generic quintic has Galois group $S_5$, the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals. The Lean proof is a 2-line `intro`/`exact`.
keyInsights: **The Galois Bridge:** `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` captures: $\alpha$ solvable by radicals over $F$ $\Rightarrow$ $\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}(\alpha))$ solvable. The contrapositive (used in `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) gives the impossibility: $\text{Gal}(q)$ not solvable $\Rightarrow$ roots of $q$ not solvable by radicals.

**Degree 5 Threshold via Derived Series:** $S_4$ has derived length 3: $D^1(S_4) = A_4$, $D^2(S_4) = V_4$, $D^3(S_4) = \{e\}$ (since $V_4$ is abelian). A composition series (refining the derived series) is $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with cyclic prime-order quotients. Contrast with $S_5$: $D^k(S_5) = A_5$ for all $k \geq 1$ (stuck — $A_5$ is perfect: $[A_5,A_5] = A_5$). This is why degree 4 has a radical formula but degree 5 does not.

**A₅ is the Key Obstruction:** $|A_5| = 60$, $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group. `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` formalizes this. The Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ makes $A_4$ solvable; no analog exists in $A_5$.

**Mathlib Integration Pattern:** The proof is a composition of Mathlib lemmas: `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` (Mathlib) + `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` (Mathlib) → `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` (3-line `intro`/`exact`). Zero sorries in 187 lines.

**S_n Unsolvability for n ≥ 5:** `symmetric_group_not_solvable` proves $\forall n \geq 5$, $S_n$ not solvable, using `Cardinal.mk (Fin n) ≥ 5` via `simp`. Instances for $S_0, S_1$ (`inferInstance`) vs the impossibility for $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ illustrate the sharp boundary.

**Original Contributions Are Wrappers:** The file's original theorems (`galois_bridge`, `symmetric_group_not_solvable`, `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) are pedagogical wrappers that make the Mathlib results explicit and user-facing — a pattern for presenting Mathlib-based formalizations.

**Jordan-Hölder Guarantees Completeness:** The analysis of $S_n$ via derived series is not ad hoc — the Jordan-Hölder theorem guarantees that any two composition series of a finite group have the same multiset of composition factors (up to isomorphism). For $S_5$, the unique composition series is $\{e\} \triangleleft A_5 \triangleleft S_5$ with factors $A_5$ (simple, order 60) and $\mathbb{Z}/2$. Since $A_5$ is non-abelian, the group is not solvable — and no alternative decomposition can avoid this obstruction. This uniqueness is what makes the degree-5 boundary absolute rather than a limitation of one particular analysis.

**Discriminant Criterion for Galois Group Computation:** The theorem `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` requires exhibiting a polynomial with non-solvable Galois group. In practice, the discriminant provides a key tool: $\text{Gal}(f) \subseteq A_n$ if and only if $\Delta(f)$ is a perfect square in $F$. For the standard example $x^5 - x - 1$, $\Delta = 2869 = 19 \times 151$, which is not a perfect square, so $\text{Gal}(x^5 - x - 1/\mathbb{Q}) \not\subseteq A_5$. Combined with irreducibility mod 2 and the existence of a 5-cycle in the Galois group (from the number of real roots), this forces $\text{Gal}(x^5 - x - 1/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$. Formalizing this computation would bridge the gap between the abstract `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` and a concrete unsolvable quintic.

**Roots of Unity as the Engine of Radical Extensions:** Every radical step $K_i \to K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ implicitly requires the $n$th roots of unity $\zeta_n = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The cyclotomic extension $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)/\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, which is abelian (hence solvable). This is the hidden ingredient in the Galois bridge: each radical step contributes an abelian Galois quotient precisely because the underlying cyclotomic symmetries are abelian (by De Moivre's formula, the $n$th roots of unity form a cyclic group under multiplication). The Abel-Ruffini impossibility arises when the polynomial's Galois group $S_5$ cannot be decomposed into such abelian layers — a failure of solvability that no choice of radical tower can circumvent.

**Kummer Theory Powers Each Radical Step:** Why is each radical extension's Galois group cyclic in the first place? Kummer theory (developed in the 1840s for cyclotomic fields, generalized by Helmut Hasse in the 1920s and reformulated cohomologically by Tate): for a field $K$ containing a primitive $n$th root of unity (with $\text{char}(K) \nmid n$), the cyclic Galois extensions of $K$ with exponent dividing $n$ correspond bijectively to subgroups of $K^*/(K^*)^n$. Concretely, $K(\sqrt[n]{a})/K$ has cyclic Galois group $\mathbb{Z}/d$ where $d$ is the order of $a$ in $K^*/(K^*)^n$. This is the precise structural fact behind the Galois bridge: a radical tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots \subset K_m$ gives composition factors that are all cyclic (after adjoining the necessary roots of unity), so the resulting Galois group is solvable. The contrapositive — non-solvable $\text{Gal}(q)$ admits no Kummer-style decomposition into cyclic radical layers — is the structural reason no radical formula can exist for the generic quintic. Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` packages this entire chain (Kummer correspondence + composition series + cyclotomic abelianness) into a single hypothesis-discharging step. The constructive converse (solvable Galois group $\Rightarrow$ explicit radical tower) is precisely the Kummer-theoretic procedure: at each composition factor $G_{i}/G_{i+1} \cong \mathbb{Z}/n_i$, the Kummer correspondence supplies the radical $\sqrt[n_i]{a_i}$ that generates the corresponding cyclic extension.

**Abel-Ruffini is Radical-Specific, Not Formula-Specific:** The impossibility is precisely about the four operations $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}\}$. Hermite (1858) showed the general quintic IS solvable using elliptic modular functions: via the icosahedral substitution $z \mapsto j(\tau)$ (the $j$-invariant), the quintic's five roots can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric series and theta functions. Klein's 1884 *Lectures on the Icosahedron* developed this fully, connecting the icosahedral symmetry group $A_5 \cong I_{60}$ to $j(\tau)$ via the relation $j(\tau) = \frac{(12g_2)^3}{\Delta}$ (with $\Delta$ the discriminant of the elliptic curve). The gallery sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07` formalizes the preparatory Bring-Jerrard reduction ($x^5 + x + t = 0$) and the Bring radical — the first step toward the elliptic solution. This insight clarifies the conceptual stakes: proving Abel-Ruffini tells us exactly *which* vocabulary of operations fails; using larger vocabularies (transcendental functions, Puiseux series, differential equations) restores solvability at the cost of leaving the radical framework.

**Arnold's Topological Proof (1963)**: Vladimir Arnold gave a completely different proof of Abel-Ruffini using the fundamental group. A radical formula for the quintic would define a continuous multi-valued function from the coefficient space $\mathbb{C}^5$ to the roots, factoring through branched covers corresponding to radical extractions. The monodromy of this function around the discriminant locus would give a solvable subgroup of the braid group, contradicting the fact that the full monodromy is $S_5$. This topological approach, made rigorous by Khovanskii (1970s-80s) via topological Galois theory, requires no algebra — only the fundamental group of configuration spaces.

**Lagrange Resolvent as Discrete Fourier Transform**: Lagrange's 1770 resolvent — the central technique behind Cardano's cubic formula and Ferrari's quartic — is, in modern language, a discrete Fourier transform over a cyclic group. Given roots $r_1, \ldots, r_n$ of a polynomial whose Galois group has a normal subgroup of cyclic quotient $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, the Lagrange resolvent $\langle \zeta, \beta\rangle = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \zeta^k \sigma^k(\beta)$ (with $\zeta$ a primitive $n$th root of unity and $\sigma$ a generator of the cyclic quotient) diagonalizes the action: by orthogonality of characters of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, the resolvent's $n$th power is fixed by the cyclic action and therefore lies in the smaller field. This is precisely the discrete Fourier inversion formula, $\hat{f}(\zeta) \hat{f}(\zeta^{-1}) \in F$ for $\hat{f}$ the DFT of a function on $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Vandermonde's 1771 solution of $x^{11} - 1 = 0$ is the textbook instance: he computed the discrete Fourier transform of the eleven roots over the cyclic group $(\mathbb{Z}/11\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. The Abel-Ruffini obstruction can therefore be rephrased: there is no DFT-style decomposition of the action of a non-solvable group like $S_5$ into cyclic pieces, because $A_5$ is perfect — no abelian quotient exists to define an analog of $\zeta$. Modern fast-Fourier-transform algorithms (Cooley-Tukey 1965) implement exactly the radical-tower structure that Galois theory shows is unavailable for non-solvable Galois groups.

**The LMFDB and Modern Computational Galois Theory**: Abel-Ruffini's qualitative impossibility has a contemporary quantitative counterpart in the LMFDB (L-functions and Modular Forms Database) and the Klüners-Malle Galois group database, which catalog Galois groups of irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$ for degree $\leq 47$ (Klüners-Malle 2001) and number-field extensions up to degree 23. As of 2024, the LMFDB lists $|S_5|/|\text{Gal}|$ statistics: among 'random' integer-coefficient quintics with $|coefficients| \leq C$, more than 99.9% have Galois group $S_5$ as $C \to \infty$ (Hilbert irreducibility quantified by van der Waerden 1934, sharpened by S. Lang 1986). The PARI/GP `polgalois` function and SAGE's `numfield_galois_group` use Stauduhar's resolvent algorithm (1973) extended by Geißler-Klüners (2000) to compute $\text{Gal}(f)$ for $\deg f \leq 23$ in milliseconds — turning Abel-Ruffini from a theoretical impossibility into an algorithmic decision procedure. This file's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` is the formal-logic analogue of this computational pipeline: given a polynomial and (algorithmic) verification that its Galois group is not solvable, conclude not solvable by radicals. Bridging Lean's pedagogical formalization with PARI/GP's algorithmic engine via verified Galois group computation is one of the major open directions for formal mathematics.

**Frobenius-Chebotarev density: the probabilistic engine of Galois group computation**: For an irreducible polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $n$ and an unramified prime $p$ (i.e., $p \nmid \text{disc}(f)$), Frobenius's 1880 theorem states that the factorization of $f \bmod p$ into irreducibles of degrees $d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k$ (with $\sum d_i = n$) corresponds to the cycle type $(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_k)$ of the Frobenius element $\text{Frob}_p \in \text{Gal}(f)$ acting on the roots. **Chebotarev's density theorem** (1922) sharpens this: the density of primes $p$ for which $\text{Frob}_p$ has a given cycle type $\tau$ equals $|\{g \in \text{Gal}(f) : g \text{ has cycle type } \tau\}| / |\text{Gal}(f)|$. This converts Abel-Ruffini's qualitative impossibility into an *effective* statistical fingerprint of the Galois group: e.g., for $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$, the proportion of primes giving 5-cycles is $24/120 = 1/5$, double-transpositions is $15/120 = 1/8$, transpositions is $10/120 = 1/12$, and the identity (full split) is $1/120$. By computing factorizations $f \bmod p$ for primes up to a few hundred and matching the empirical cycle-type distribution against the lookup tables of cycle-index polynomials (one per transitive subgroup of $S_n$), Stauduhar's algorithm and its descendants identify $\text{Gal}(f)$ with high confidence. The crucial observation: the cycle-index distribution of $S_5$ differs from every solvable transitive subgroup of $S_5$ — verifying $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$ via a few dozen modular factorizations is enough to conclude (modulo the density bound) that $f$ is not solvable by radicals. The non-solvability of $S_5$ thus becomes algorithmically detectable: irreducibility mod 2 alone (giving a 5-cycle in $\text{Gal}(f)$, hence transitivity) plus an even number of complex roots (giving a transposition) suffices to force $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$ via Galois's theorem on transitive subgroups of $S_p$ containing a transposition and a $p$-cycle. Mathlib has elementary $p$-adic theory but lacks Chebotarev — formalizing it would unlock effective Galois group computation in Lean and complete the bridge from `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` to verified concrete unsolvable polynomials.

**Geometry of Solvability: The Cube Solves, the Icosahedron Does Not**: The solvability of $S_4$ versus the non-solvability of $A_5$ has a striking geometric interpretation through the rotation groups of the Platonic solids. The rotation group of the cube (equivalently, the octahedron, by duality) is $\text{Rot}(\square) \cong S_4$, acting faithfully by permuting the four space diagonals of the cube. The rotation group of the regular tetrahedron is $\text{Rot}(\triangle) \cong A_4$, realized inside $\text{Rot}(\square)$ as the rotations of the cube that preserve a chosen inscribed tetrahedron. Inside $A_4$ sits the Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e, R_x, R_y, R_z\}$: the three 180° rotations about the cube's face-axes (perpendicular axes through opposite face-centers), which fix the inscribed tetrahedron *as a set* and form a normal subgroup of $A_4$ because the eight 120° body-diagonal rotations conjugate them to one another. The full chain $S_4 \triangleright A_4 \triangleright V_4 \triangleright \langle R_x \rangle \triangleright \{e\}$ thus corresponds geometrically to: cube rotations ⊃ tetrahedral rotations ⊃ face-axis 180° rotations ⊃ a single axis ⊃ identity. Each abelian quotient ($\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/3, \mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/2$) supplies a radical extraction step — which is *exactly why* the quartic has Ferrari's formula. **The icosahedron tells the opposite story.** Its rotation group $I \cong A_5$ is simple — no proper nontrivial normal subgroup exists. Geometrically there is no analogue of the inscribed-tetrahedron picture: every rotation orbit of a non-identity element generates the full group. This geometric simplicity is the intuitive content of the non-solvability obstruction this entry's `symmetric_group_not_solvable` formalizes algebraically — the Klein four-group inside $A_4$ has no icosahedral counterpart inside $A_5$. Klein (1884) turned this perspective into a positive solution method: since the radical chain available for the cube/tetrahedron is missing for the icosahedron, he replaced it with an analytic substitute, threading the quintic through the icosahedral $j$-line $\mathbb{P}^1/A_5$ via hypergeometric uniformization. The cube/icosahedron dichotomy is thus the geometric face of the algebraic threshold at $n = 5$: the same Platonic solids that classify rotational symmetries in three dimensions also classify the boundary between radical solvability and impossibility.

sections.title: The Galois Bridge
sections.summary: Part II docstring and `galois_bridge`: if $\alpha$ is solvable by radicals over $F$ and $\alpha$ is a root of irreducible $q$, then `IsSolvable q.Gal`. One-line proof: `solvableByRad.isSolvable' hq hroot hrad`. The key bridge between field theory and group theory.
sections.mathContext: This theorem captures the hard direction of Galois's fundamental theorem: an element expressible via field operations and $n$th roots forces its minimal polynomial's Galois group to be solvable (admit a composition series with abelian factors). The converse — solvable Galois group implies solvable by radicals — is also true but not needed for the impossibility result. The contrapositive used later is: if $\text{Gal}(q)$ is not solvable, then no root of $q$ is expressible by radicals.

sections.title: S_n Not Solvable; A₅ Simple
sections.summary: Part III: four theorems — `symmetric_group_not_solvable` ($n \geq 5 \Rightarrow S_n$ not solvable, via `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` and `Cardinal.mk (Fin n) \geq 5`), `s5_not_solvable` (n=5, using `le_rfl`), `s6_not_solvable` (n=6), `a5_is_simple` (`IsSimpleGroup (alternatingGroup (Fin 5))`).
sections.mathContext: The non-solvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$ is a pure group-theoretic fact: the derived series of $S_5$ is $S_5 \supset A_5 \supset A_5 \supset \cdots$ because $A_5$ is perfect ($A_5 = [A_5, A_5]$). This contrasts with $S_4$, where the derived series reaches $\{e\}$ in exactly 3 steps: $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ (since $[V_4,V_4] = \{e\}$ — the Klein four-group is abelian). A composition series of $S_4$ refines this to $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with 4 simple quotients. The simplicity of $A_5$ (order 60, the smallest non-abelian simple group) is the critical obstruction: a simple non-abelian group has no proper normal subgroups, so the derived series cannot descend.

sections.mathContext: The Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is the key structural feature making $S_4$ solvable: it is a normal subgroup of $A_4$ with quotient $\mathbb{Z}/3$, and $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ is abelian. No such subgroup exists in $A_5$: any non-trivial normal subgroup of $A_5$ would have to be a union of conjugacy classes of sizes 1, 15, 20, 12, 12 (summing to 60), but no such sub-sum (including 1) divides 60 and yields a normal subgroup.

conclusion.summary:
This formalization is Wiedijk theorem #16 — one of the 100 landmark mathematical results tracked for formal proof. It demonstrates one of mathematics' most beautiful connections: the solution of polynomial equations reduces to group theory. Galois's insight that symmetry groups control solvability unified algebra in a profound way, transforming a 300-year search for a quintic formula into a structural impossibility with a clean mathematical explanation.

The Lean formalization in 187 lines (zero sorries, zero axioms) works as a pedagogical walkthrough: the three original theorems (`galois_bridge`, `symmetric_group_not_solvable`, `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) are wrappers composing Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`, `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`, and `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. The heart of the argument — `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — is a 2-line `intro`/`exact` contrapositive.

This entry anchors a rich cluster of related gallery proofs: the complete solvability classification $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ (`abel-ruffini-galois-extensions`), the full bidirectional Galois criterion (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-03`), a concrete unsolvable quintic $x^5 - 4x + 2$ with $\text{Gal} \cong S_5$ (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), and the Bring-Jerrard reduction showing the quintic's 'beyond-radicals' solution via the Bring radical (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`). Together they build a complete formal picture of polynomial solvability from foundations to frontier.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Galois theory has far-reaching consequences:

1. CONSTRUCTIBILITY: Similar techniques prove that angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible with compass and straightedge — both reduce to showing that the relevant Galois group is not a 2-group.

2. INVERSE GALOIS PROBLEM: Which groups appear as Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$? This remains open for many groups. Shafarevich proved every solvable group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$, but the general case is wide open.

3. ALGEBRAIC NUMBER THEORY: Galois groups of field extensions are central to understanding number fields and their arithmetic. Class field theory classifies abelian extensions via Artin reciprocity.

4. MODERN ALGEBRA: Galois's ideas pioneered the abstract study of groups, fields, and their relationships — the foundation of modern algebra.

5. SPECIFIC SOLUTIONS: While the general quintic is unsolvable, specific quintics may be solvable. Galois theory tells us exactly which ones: a polynomial is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable.

6. DIFFERENTIAL GALOIS THEORY: Picard-Vessiot theory extends Galois's framework from polynomial equations to linear differential equations. Just as Abel-Ruffini shows certain algebraic equations cannot be solved by radicals (because $S_5$ is not solvable), Liouville's theorem in differential algebra shows certain integrals — such as $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$ — cannot be expressed in elementary functions, proved by analyzing the differential Galois group of the associated equation. The parallel is precise: 'solvable by radicals' becomes 'expressible in elementary functions', and 'solvable Galois group' becomes 'solvable differential Galois group'.

**Broader Connections**:

7. IMPOSSIBILITY PARADIGM: Abel-Ruffini inaugurated a tradition of impossibility proofs that extends through Lindemann's transcendence of $e$ and $\pi$ (1882), Cantor's diagonal argument proving the uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$ (1891), Gödel's incompleteness (1931), Turing's halting problem (1936), and Matiyasevich's negative resolution of Hilbert's tenth problem (1970). Each shows that some natural class of problems admits no universal solution within a given formal framework. Cantor's diagonal method, in particular, became the template for both Gödel's and Turing's proofs.

8. TRANSCENDENCE HIERARCHY: Abel-Ruffini's impossibility (roots not expressible by radicals) sits between irrationality ($\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$, c. 500 BCE) and transcendence ($e, \pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, 1882) in a hierarchy of expressibility barriers.

9. FEIT-THOMPSON AND THE ODD ORDER THEOREM: The Feit-Thompson theorem (1963) — every group of odd order is solvable — is the deepest generalization of the solvability concept central to Abel-Ruffini. It implies that any polynomial whose Galois group has odd order is solvable by radicals, and its 255-page proof launched the classification of finite simple groups. The formalization of Feit-Thompson in Coq (Gonthier et al., 2013) was a landmark in formal verification.

10. CLASSIFICATION OF FINITE SIMPLE GROUPS: The simplicity of $A_5$, which drives Abel-Ruffini, was the first step in the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) — completed c. 2004. The CFSG shows that every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating ($A_n$, $n \geq 5$), a group of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups. Abel-Ruffini's obstruction ($A_5$ is simple) is thus the first instance of the alternating family in the classification.

11. TOPOLOGICAL PROOF VIA MONODROMY: V.I. Arnold (1963) discovered a purely topological proof of Abel-Ruffini that bypasses abstract algebra entirely. As the coefficients of a polynomial vary continuously along loops in coefficient space $\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Delta$ (where $\Delta$ is the discriminant locus), the roots undergo continuous permutations — monodromy — forming a representation of the fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Delta)$ into $S_n$. For the generic quintic, this monodromy representation is surjective onto $S_5$. Since each radical extraction $z \mapsto z^{1/n}$ contributes only cyclic monodromy ($\mathbb{Z}/n$), any radical expression has solvable monodromy group. The non-solvability of $S_5$ therefore obstructs radical expressibility — purely from continuity and the topology of branched coverings, with no mention of fields, extensions, or automorphisms. Arnold originally presented this proof to Moscow high school students in 1963, demonstrating that the impossibility of the quintic can be understood with minimal algebraic prerequisites.
openQuestions: **Constructive direction of the Galois bridge**: `galois_bridge` proves the forward implication — solvability by radicals implies solvable Galois group — and the proof uses this direction contrapositively. The converse is equally important and more constructive: given a composition series $\{e\} = G_k \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_0 = \text{Gal}(q)$ with cyclic quotients $G_{i}/G_{i+1} \cong \mathbb{Z}/n_i$, Galois's original argument constructs a radical tower via Kummer theory at each step — the cyclic extension corresponds to adjoining an $n_i$th root. Can Lean formalize this constructive direction explicitly for a specific solvable polynomial — for example, exhibiting the complete radical tower for $x^4 - 2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ (Galois group $D_4$, solvable derived series $D_4 \supset \mathbb{Z}/4 \supset \mathbb{Z}/2 \supset \{e\}$, corresponding radical tower $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2}, i)$) — making the path from solvable group to radical tower machine-verified and completing the bidirectional Galois correspondence for a concrete case?

**[Addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02`]** Mathlib instances for $S_2, S_3, S_4$ were missing at time of writing. The sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02` fills this gap: it proves $S_2, S_3, S_4$ are solvable via explicit derived series arguments and establishes the bidirectional theorem $S_n$ is solvable iff $n \leq 4$. The alternating-group analogue ($A_n$ solvable iff $n \leq 4$) is proved in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-02-oq-02`.

**[Partially addressed in `inverse-galois-oq-02`]** The Inverse Galois Problem — whether every finite group appears as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ — is a deep open problem. The gallery entry `inverse-galois-oq-02` formalizes the Mathieu group $M_{23}$ (the only sporadic simple group not yet known to be realizable as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$), proving it is perfect, non-solvable, and beyond the reach of Shafarevich's theorem (which applies only to solvable groups). Can further partial results be formalized in Lean? Key candidates: every abelian group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ by Kronecker-Weber; every $S_n$ is realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$ by Hilbert irreducibility (Serre's *Topics in Galois Theory*); and every finite quotient of the absolute Galois group $\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ is conjectured to be realizable.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04`]** The file relies on `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` and `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` as black boxes. The sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04` exposes the internal proof chain from $A_5$ simplicity through the derived series to the Abel-Ruffini impossibility as individually named pedagogical theorems. The deeper question — fully exposing the Mathlib proofs of `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` and `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` themselves as individual Lean lemmas with explicit composition factor analysis — remains open for a fully self-contained formalization.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`]** Charles Hermite (1858) showed that the general quintic *can* be solved using elliptic modular functions — bypassing the radical barrier by expanding the class of allowed operations. The sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07` formalizes the Bring-Jerrard reduction (Tschirnhaus substitution eliminating the $x^4$ term) and proves the Bring radical $\text{BR}(t)$ — the unique real root of $x^5 + x + t = 0$ — exists and is strictly anti-monotone. The full elliptic modular solution (connecting $\text{BR}(t)$ to $j(\tau)$ via hypergeometric functions) remains to be formalized.

In positive characteristic $p > 0$, the Abel-Ruffini picture changes dramatically: the Abhyankar conjecture (proved by Raynaud 1994, Harbater 1994) characterizes which finite groups occur as Galois groups of covers of $\mathbb{A}^1$ over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p$ — every group whose $p$-Sylow subgroup is a $p$-group appears. Unlike characteristic 0, where $S_5$'s non-solvability creates an absolute barrier, in characteristic 5 the Galois theory of polynomial equations behaves quite differently because Artin-Schreier extensions replace radical extensions. Can Lean formalize how the Abel-Ruffini impossibility is characteristic-dependent?

**Galois group computation and the resolvent method**: `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` requires exhibiting a polynomial with non-solvable Galois group to give a concrete unsolvable quintic. In practice, this is done by Stauduhar's algorithm (1973) — factoring resolvent polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$ to identify $\text{Gal}(f)$ as a subgroup of $S_n$. For $f = x^5 - x - 1$, the resolvent factors show $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$. Can Lean formalize any step of this computation: either the construction of a resolvent for a specific polynomial, or the verification that a given resolvent does not factor, establishing that $\text{Gal}(f) \not\subseteq A_5$? A formalized resolvent computation would connect `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` to a machine-verified unsolvable quintic, closing the gap between the abstract impossibility and the concrete case that ab initio numerical methods face. **[Partial progress in the gallery]** The cubic case is now well-developed: `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal` computes $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 6X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ for $\cos(20°)$, `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03-oq-01` computes $|\text{Gal}(4X^2 + 2X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 2$ for $\cos(72°)$, and `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01-oq-01` parameterizes a unified cubic Galois computation across $p \in \{3, 7\}$. All current gallery Galois group computations land in small solvable groups; the unsolvable-quintic case (e.g., $\text{Gal}(x^5 - x - 1) = S_5$ via resolvent factorization, or $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2) = S_5$ via galActionHom in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`) remains the natural next step to scale this methodology beyond the radical-solvable regime.

**Arnold-Khovanskii topological proof**: Can Arnold's topological proof of Abel-Ruffini (using monodromy groups of algebraic functions and the fundamental group of $\mathbb{C}^5 \setminus \Delta$ where $\Delta$ is the discriminant locus) be formalized in Lean 4? This requires topological machinery — fundamental groups, covering spaces, monodromy representations — that is partially in Mathlib (e.g., `π₁`) but not yet connected to algebraic functions. Khovanskii's *Topological Galois Theory* (2014) provides the fully rigorous framework: a monodromy representation $\rho : \pi_1(\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Sigma) \to S_n$ with non-solvable image obstructs expressibility in finite terms, and the same machinery extends to differential Galois theory (giving Liouville-style integration impossibility). A Lean formalization would require connecting Mathlib's covering space theory to Polynomial.Gal via the discriminant locus.

**Differential Galois theory and Liouville's theorem on integration**: The direct analog of Abel-Ruffini for integration — Liouville's theorem (1840) that $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ cannot be expressed in elementary functions — is proved via differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot theory). Can this be formalized in Lean 4? It would require differential ring extensions and a differential analog of the Galois correspondence, which are not yet in Mathlib.

**Chebotarev density in Lean**: Chebotarev's density theorem (1922) is the engine of computational Galois theory — the cycle-type distribution of Frobenius elements over primes equals the cycle-type distribution of group elements. Mathlib formalizes the elementary theory of Frobenius elements (`NumberField.Frobenius`, in the unramified case via the decomposition group) but does not yet have Chebotarev. A Lean proof would require: (1) formalizing the Artin $L$-function (a major undertaking); (2) following Lagarias-Odlyzko's effective version (1977); or (3) the elementary 'first density theorem' (Frobenius's original 1880 form, restricted to cycle types corresponding to conjugacy classes). Even just Frobenius's density — without effective bounds — would let Lean verify $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$ for explicit $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ via a finite computation, closing the loop on `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` for concrete unsolvable polynomials. This is arguably the highest-leverage open question for formal Galois theory: a modest (but technical) formalization unlocks effective verification of Abel-Ruffini for any concrete $f$.

The barrier is specific to the radical operations (+, -, ×, ÷, ⁿ√), not to all closed-form representations

Sylow's theorems (Wiedijk #72) provide the group-theoretic machinery underlying the simplicity of A₅ — the cornerstone of Abel-Ruffini's impossibility. Sylow counting for A₅ (order 60 = 2²·3·5) shows the five-Sylow subgroup count must satisfy n₅ ≡ 1 (mod 5) and n₅ ∣ 12, giving n₅ ∈ {1, 6}; n₅ = 1 would make the Sylow 5-subgroup normal in A₅, contradicting simplicity, so n₅ = 6. The conjugacy class approach used in `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` directly instantiates the same structural constraints that Sylow's theorems systematize for all finite groups.
Lagrange's theorem on subgroup orders underpins the group-theoretic machinery: the derived series, composition factors, and index calculations used to analyze S₅ and A₅

Vieta's formulas express polynomial coefficients as elementary symmetric functions of roots — this is precisely why the Galois group acts by permutations on roots. The failure of $S_5$-solvability means the elementary symmetric functions of quintic roots cannot be 'unscrambled' using radicals

The primitive root theorem — $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic of order $p-1$ — is the algebraic engine behind cyclotomic Galois theory: $\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)/\mathbb{Q}) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, which is abelian. This cyclic (hence solvable) Galois group explains why each root-of-unity extraction in a radical tower contributes an abelian Galois group quotient. Abel-Ruffini's impossibility arises when the full Galois group $S_5$ cannot be decomposed into such abelian cyclic layers

Sits one level above Abel-Ruffini in the expressibility hierarchy: Abel-Ruffini shows certain algebraic numbers escape radical expressions, while Hermite-Lindemann shows $e^\alpha$ is transcendental for nonzero algebraic $\alpha$. Hermite himself showed the quintic IS solvable via elliptic modular functions (1858), demonstrating the barrier is specific to radicals

Proves Vieta's formulas for the three Cardano roots of $x^3 + px + q = 0$ (sum $= 0$, pairwise products $= p$, triple product $= -q$) and the complete factorization into linear factors. This is the positive constructive counterpart to Abel-Ruffini: Cardano's formula works because $S_3$ is solvable ($S_3 \triangleright A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3 \triangleright \{e\}$), and Vieta's formulas express the symmetric functions of roots that the Galois group permutes

Formalizes the discriminant $\Delta = -4p^3 - 27q^2 = (x_1-x_2)^2(x_1-x_3)^2(x_2-x_3)^2$ of the depressed cubic $x^3+px+q=0$ and its connection to root nature. The discriminant criterion is central to Abel-Ruffini: $\text{Gal}(f) \subseteq A_n$ iff $\Delta(f)$ is a perfect square in $F$. For the quintic examples used to instantiate `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — e.g., $x^5 - x - 1$ with $\Delta = 2869 = 19 \times 151$ (not a perfect square) — the non-square discriminant immediately forces $\text{Gal}(f) \not\subseteq A_5$. This cubic formalization provides the foundational discriminant machinery on which quintic Galois group computations build

Formalizes the casus irreducibilis: when $x^3+px+q=0$ has three distinct real roots ($\Delta > 0$), Cardano's formula necessarily involves non-real complex cube roots even though all roots are real. This illustrates that radical expressibility (Abel-Ruffini) is subtler than existence of real solutions: even when a radical formula exists (as for the cubic, since $S_3$ is solvable), the formula may require complex intermediate values. The casus irreducibilis foreshadows Abel-Ruffini's impossibility at degree 5, where no radical formula exists at all

Proves that Ferrari's resolvent cubic for the quartic reduces to a depressed cubic solvable by Cardano's formula, completing the quartic-cubic-Cardano solution chain. Lagrange's 1770 analysis (described in this entry's historicalContext) studied resolvents precisely: the resolvent of a cubic has degree 2 (solvable by square roots), the resolvent of a quartic has degree 3 (solvable by Cardano), but the resolvent of a quintic has degree 6 — higher, not lower — which is the sign that no radical formula can exist. This entry formalizes the quartic resolvent step that succeeds; Abel-Ruffini explains why the corresponding quintic step fails

The irrationality of $\sqrt[n]{m}$ for non-perfect-power $m$ is the simplest instance of the radical extension phenomenon central to Abel-Ruffini: each adjunction $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[n]{m})/\mathbb{Q}$ produces a degree-$n$ extension with cyclic Galois group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ (solvable). Abel-Ruffini's impossibility arises when the full Galois group $S_5$ cannot be decomposed into such cyclic layers — the irrationality barrier ($\sqrt[n]{m} \notin \mathbb{Q}$) is the first level of the expressibility hierarchy discussed in the conclusion

The irrationality of $\sqrt{2}$ (c. 500 BCE) is the earliest impossibility result in the expressibility hierarchy discussed in the conclusion: $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$ shows certain quantities escape rational expressions. Abel-Ruffini extends this paradigm one level higher: certain algebraic quantities escape radical expressions. The progression irrationality → radical inexpressibility → transcendence ($e, \pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$) forms the expressibility hierarchy that Abel-Ruffini occupies at the middle level

Formalizes that the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt{2}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $X^2 - 2$. The `galois_bridge` theorem in this entry takes the minimal polynomial $\text{minpoly}_F(\alpha)$ as a key input — this entry makes that input concrete for the simplest radical extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})/\mathbb{Q}$. The Galois group of $X^2 - 2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (cyclic, solvable), confirming that $\sqrt{2}$ is solvable by radicals in exact alignment with `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`'s contrapositive

Each step $K_i \to K_i(\sqrt[n]{a})$ in a radical tower requires that $X^n - a$ is irreducible over $K_i$ — exactly the Eisenstein-type irreducibility this entry formalizes. The Galois group of $X^2 - n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (solvable), providing a gallery-verified instance of the abelian Galois quotient at each radical step

Formalizes that $\text{minpoly}_{\mathbb{Q}}(m^{1/n}) = X^n - m$ whenever $m$ has a prime factor $p$ with $p \mid m$ but $p^2 \nmid m$ (Eisenstein at $p$). This is the exact polynomial used in each radical extension step of the Galois bridge: when $\alpha = m^{1/n}$ is adjoined to build a radical tower, `galois_bridge` applies to $q = X^n - m$ with $\text{aeval}\,\alpha\,q = 0$. The Galois group of $X^n - m$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is metacyclic (a subgroup of the dihedral group $D_n$) and hence solvable — machine-verified proof that each individual radical step contributes a solvable Galois quotient to the tower

The Wantzel-Galois characterization of constructibility: an algebraic number $\alpha$ is constructible iff $\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha))$ is a 2-group. This is directly parallel to Abel-Ruffini's characterization of radical solvability: $\alpha$ is solvable by radicals iff $\text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_{\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha))$ is solvable. Both use Galois groups to convert geometric/algebraic impossibility questions into group-theoretic conditions — 2-groups for constructibility, solvable groups for radical solvability

Hall's theorem (1928) characterizes solvable groups positively: a finite group is solvable iff it has Hall subgroups of every coprime order. This provides a structural 'positive test' for solvability complementing the impossibility at degree 5 — S₅ has no subgroup of order 15 (max element order is 6), so S₅ fails Hall's criterion

Proves A₅ ≅ Gal(x⁵-5x⁴+10x³-10x²+25x-5/ℚ) via Eisenstein at $p=5$ and Sylow theory. Since A₅ is not solvable (the simplicity of A₅ is the key obstruction in Abel-Ruffini), applying `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` yields a concrete quintic whose roots are not expressible by radicals. Provides an alternative concrete witness to `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`'s S₅-based example, completing the picture: both A₅ and S₅ appear as Galois groups over ℚ and both obstruct radical solvability

Formalizes the Mathieu group $M_{23}$ — the only sporadic simple group not yet known to be a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$. Proves $M_{23}$ is perfect ($[M_{23}, M_{23}] = M_{23}$), non-solvable (so Shafarevich's theorem, which covers only solvable groups, does not apply), with $|M_{23}| = 2^7 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$. Directly instantiates the open Inverse Galois Problem discussed in this entry's implications: while Shafarevich proved every solvable group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$, non-solvable sporadic groups like $M_{23}$ remain an active open frontier

Formalizes the orbit enumeration formula $n_p = [G : N_G(P)]$ via the orbit-stabilizer theorem: all Sylow $p$-subgroups form a single conjugation orbit $\{gPg^{-1} \mid g \in G\}$, and the normality criterion $n_p = 1 \Leftrightarrow P \trianglelefteq G$ is proved explicitly. This is the precise mechanism underlying the Sylow counting argument for $A_5$ simplicity: $n_5$ divides 12 and $n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$ forces $n_5 \in \{1, 6\}$; the criterion $n_5 = 1 \Rightarrow P_5 \trianglelefteq A_5$ contradicts simplicity, so $n_5 = 6$. `sylow-theorem-oq-04` applies this formula concretely to $A_5$; this entry establishes the formula in full generality.

Constructs from scratch the Sylow-theoretic proof that $A_5$ (order $60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$) is simple: computes Sylow numbers $n_2 = 5$, $n_3 = 10$, $n_5 = 6$ by exhaustive enumeration, shows no Sylow subgroup is normal, and confirms simplicity via conjugacy class analysis. This is the group-theoretic keystone of Abel-Ruffini: the Lean proof in this entry delegates $A_5$ simplicity to Mathlib's `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`, while `sylow-theorem-oq-04` provides the elementary first-principles verification — together they demonstrate how the same mathematical fact can be accessed at both foundational and library levels

An independent Sylow-based formalization of $A_5$ simplicity via conjugacy class arithmetic: the five conjugacy classes of $A_5$ have sizes $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$ summing to 60, and none of the proper subsets including $\{1\}$ is closed under conjugation, ruling out any proper nontrivial normal subgroup. This corroborates the $A_5$ simplicity that drives the non-solvability of $S_5$ in this entry, and illustrates the combinatorial power of Sylow theory: the same impossibility result proved via group orders and counting is the foundation of the algebraic impossibility of solving quintics by radicals

Liouville's theorem (1844) constructs the first explicit transcendental numbers — Liouville numbers such as $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 10^{-k!}$ — via rational approximation bounds. This sits one level above Abel-Ruffini in the expressibility hierarchy: Abel-Ruffini shows certain algebraic quantities escape radical expressions (middle tier), while Liouville's theorem demonstrates quantities that escape all algebraic equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ (top tier). The hierarchy $\mathbb{Q} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_{\text{rad}} \subsetneq \overline{\mathbb{Q}} \subsetneq \mathbb{C}$ — rationals, radical-solvable algebraics, all algebraics, all complex numbers — has Abel-Ruffini as the gap between the first and second tiers, and Liouville/Hermite-Lindemann as the gap between the second and third

Proves the algebraic bridge between Cardano's cubic formula and Ferrari's quartic method: the Tschirnhaus substitution $m = t - 5p/6$ reduces Ferrari's resolvent cubic to depressed form, so Cardano's formula directly supplies the required resolvent root. This is the last successful resolvent step before Abel-Ruffini's barrier: Lagrange (1770) discovered that the resolvent of a quintic has degree 6 (higher than 5), so no such reduction exists for degree 5. The chain cubic resolvent (degree 2, quadratic formula) → quartic resolvent (degree 3, Cardano) → quintic resolvent (degree 6, no reduction) is the historical precursor to Abel's impossibility proof — formalizing each step clarifies precisely where and why the radical method fails

The Kronecker-Weber theorem — every abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is cyclotomic — is the positive counterpart to Abel-Ruffini: while Abel-Ruffini shows non-solvable Galois groups (like $S_5$) block radical solvability entirely, Kronecker-Weber shows all abelian Galois groups correspond to cyclotomic extensions generated by roots of unity. Kronecker's Jugendtraum (Hilbert's 12th problem) generalizes this to abelian extensions of imaginary quadratic fields via complex multiplication. Together they frame the Galois-theoretic classification at both extremes: Abel-Ruffini identifies the obstruction (non-solvable groups), Kronecker-Weber and class field theory classify the well-behaved case (abelian groups)

Artin reciprocity (the resolution of Hilbert's 9th problem) provides the definitive classification of abelian extensions via class field theory: every abelian extension of a number field is a class field, and its Galois group is isomorphic to a quotient of the idèle class group. Abel-Ruffini characterizes the opposite extreme — non-abelian (non-solvable) Galois groups like $S_5$ block radical solvability entirely. The implications section notes that class field theory classifies abelian extensions via Artin reciprocity; this entry formalizes the key structural results underlying that classification

Descartes' rule of signs is a key tool for computing the Galois group of a specific quintic needed to instantiate `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`. For $x^5 - x - 1$, the rule shows exactly three positive and zero negative real roots; the polynomial therefore has three real and two complex-conjugate roots. Complex conjugation then contributes a transposition to $\text{Gal}(x^5-x-1/\mathbb{Q})$, and combined with the 5-cycle arising from irreducibility over $\mathbb{F}_2$, forces $\text{Gal}(x^5-x-1/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$ — completing the proof that $x^5 - x - 1$ has roots not expressible by radicals. Root-counting and group theory combine to give the concrete witness this entry's abstract theorem requires

The transcendence of $e$ (Hermite, 1873) sits one level above Abel-Ruffini in the expressibility hierarchy discussed in this entry's implications: Abel-Ruffini shows certain algebraic quantities (quintic roots) escape radical expressions, while Hermite's theorem places $e$ outside all algebraic equations over $\mathbb{Q}$. The progression — irrationality ($\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$) $\subset$ radical inexpressibility (Abel-Ruffini) $\subset$ algebraic inexpressibility ($e, \pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$) — marks successive enlargements of the vocabulary of expressibility. Hermite's proof technique (approximating $e$ by rational functions and bounding remainders) is a precursor to Lindemann's 1882 transcendence of $\pi$, completing the impossibility of squaring the circle

The transcendence of $\pi$ (Lindemann, 1882) sits alongside $e$-transcendence in the expressibility hierarchy: both $e$ and $\pi$ lie above all algebraic quantities, while Abel-Ruffini's quintic roots are algebraic but not radical. Lindemann's result — and its generalization Hermite-Lindemann — immediately implies the impossibility of squaring the circle (constructing a segment of length $\sqrt{\pi}$ from a unit segment). Together `e-transcendental` and `pi-transcendental` in the gallery bracket the algebraic inexpressibility tier: radical-inexpressible algebraic roots (Abel-Ruffini) live strictly between the rationals and the transcendentals. The Hermite-Lindemann theorem formalizes the precise statement: if $\alpha$ is algebraic and nonzero, then $e^\alpha$ is transcendental; hence $e^{i\pi} = -1$ (Euler's identity) forces $i\pi$ to be transcendental (since $-1$ is algebraic), confirming $\pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$

The Gelfond-Schneider theorem (Hilbert's 7th problem, resolved 1934) proves $a^b$ is transcendental for algebraic $a \neq 0, 1$ and algebraic irrational $b$. It occupies the transcendental tier of the expressibility hierarchy where Abel-Ruffini occupies the radical tier: Abel-Ruffini blocks radical representations of certain polynomial roots (group-theoretic obstruction: $S_5$ not solvable), while Gelfond-Schneider blocks algebraic representation of $a^b$ entirely (transcendence barrier). Both results demonstrate that natural-looking expressions — $\alpha^{1/5}$ for Abel-Ruffini, $2^{\sqrt{2}}$ for Gelfond-Schneider — escape their respective formal frameworks. Gelfond-Schneider applies directly to the quintic's solution via elliptic modular functions: the Hermite-Klein solution involves $j(\tau)$ for $\tau$ algebraic, and the $j$-invariant involves quantities that Gelfond-Schneider classifies as transcendental

The eigenvalues of an $n \times n$ matrix $M$ are the roots of its characteristic polynomial $\chi_M(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - M)$, a degree-$n$ polynomial. Abel-Ruffini implies that for $n \geq 5$, these eigenvalues generally have no closed-form expression in radicals — yet Cayley-Hamilton guarantees $\chi_M(M) = 0$ regardless. This contrast between algebraic satisfaction (the matrix annihilates its own characteristic polynomial) and radical inexpressibility (the eigenvalues cannot be named by radicals for general $n \geq 5$) illustrates the distinction between existence (eigenvalues exist in $\mathbb{C}$ by FTA) and expressibility (they cannot always be written using $+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\phantom{x}}$). Cayley-Hamilton is thus the linear-algebraic dual of Abel-Ruffini: one guarantees a polynomial is satisfied, the other shows the roots of a polynomial need not be expressible in radicals

Proves Vieta's formulas for the general cubic $x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c = (x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)$ over any commutative ring: $a = -(r_1+r_2+r_3)$, $b = r_1r_2+r_1r_3+r_2r_3$, $c = -r_1r_2r_3$. Machine-verifies the foundational reason Galois groups act by permutations: the polynomial coefficients are the elementary symmetric polynomials $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ in the roots, hence invariant under every permutation of the roots — so the Galois group permutes roots while fixing coefficients in the base field. Abel-Ruffini's impossibility for degree $\geq 5$ amounts to: $S_5$ permutes five roots, but no composition of $+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\phantom{x}}$ can extract individual roots from the symmetric-polynomial data encoded in the four coefficients, precisely because $S_5$ is not solvable. This entry bridges the abstract Abel-Ruffini story to the concrete degree-3 case, illustrating why symmetric polynomial invariance is both what makes Galois theory work (coefficients are symmetric functions) and what prevents radical solving in degree 5 (the symmetry group is too large and non-solvable)

Turing's 1936 undecidability of the halting problem is the computational instantiation of the impossibility paradigm that Abel-Ruffini inaugurated: Abel proved certain algebraic roots cannot be *named* by radicals (an expressibility barrier arising from $S_5$'s non-solvability), Turing proved certain functions cannot be *computed* by any algorithm (a decidability barrier arising from self-referential diagonalization). Both results show that a natural class of problems admits no universal solution within a given formal framework — and both use contradiction against a hypothetical universal method. The implications section cites the halting problem as a direct methodological descendant of Abel's impossibility proof

Matiyasevich's 1970 negative resolution of Hilbert's 10th problem — no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation $p(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = 0$ has integer solutions — is the arithmetic instantiation of Abel-Ruffini's impossibility paradigm: Abel proved that polynomial roots cannot generally be *expressed* by radicals (group-theoretic obstruction: $S_5$ not solvable), while MRDP proves that Diophantine solvability cannot be *decided* by any algorithm (via the equivalence of Diophantine sets and recursively enumerable sets). Both concern polynomial equations, but at different levels: Abel-Ruffini blocks closed-form representation of roots, MRDP blocks algorithmic determination of existence of roots

Hilbert's 13th problem asks whether solutions of degree-7 polynomials can be expressed as superpositions of continuous functions of two variables — extending Abel-Ruffini's expressibility question from radical operations to function composition. The Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem (1956-57) resolves the continuous case positively: every continuous function of $n$ variables CAN be represented using functions of one variable. But the algebraic version — whether roots of degree-7 polynomials require algebraic functions of three or more variables — relates to the Tschirnhaus transformations used in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`'s Bring-Jerrard reduction, which eliminates variables from quintics using algebraic substitutions. The classical chain: Bring-Jerrard reduces to $x^5 + x + t$ (one parameter), but the analogous reduction for degree 7 was Hilbert's original concern

Concrete Galois group computation in the gallery: proves $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 6X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ for the minimal polynomial of $\cos(20°)$ via Eisenstein irreducibility on the shifted polynomial $X^3 - 6X^2 + 9X - 3$ and a splitting-field analysis showing all three roots lie in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. Demonstrates the same toolkit (Eisenstein criterion, splitting field equality, $|\text{Gal}| = [\text{splitting field} : F]$) that the open question on Galois group computation calls for in the quintic case. Here the computed Galois group $\mathbb{Z}/3$ is solvable, so the cubic IS solvable by radicals (consistent with Cardano); the analogous quintic computation would yield a non-solvable Galois group and instantiate `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`

Concrete Galois group computation: $|\text{Gal}(4X^2 + 2X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 2$ for the minimal polynomial of $\cos(72°) = \cos(2\pi/5)$. Establishes irreducibility via Eisenstein on the shifted polynomial $4X^2 + 10X + 5$ (Eisenstein at $p = 5$), then bounds the splitting field by exhibiting both roots $\cos(72°), \cos(144°)$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\cos(72°))$. Illustrates the $p = 5$ instance of $|\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\cos(2\pi/p))/\mathbb{Q})| = (p-1)/2$. As with all gallery Galois group computations to date, the result is a small abelian (hence solvable) group; the methodology scales but no formalization yet realizes the non-solvable case the Abel-Ruffini contrapositive demands

Parameterized Galois group computation across two distinct cubic minimal polynomials: both $\cos(20°)$ ($8X^3 - 6X - 1$) and $\cos(\pi/7)$ ($8X^3 - 4X^2 - 4X + 1$) have Galois groups of order 3 over $\mathbb{Q}$. Introduces `trisectionPoly p` and `eisensteinCubic p` parameterized by Eisenstein prime $p \in \{3, 7\}$, with all theorems unified via `rcases hp with rfl | rfl`. Demonstrates a pattern relevant to formalizing Abel-Ruffini's quintic instantiation: parameterized polynomial families with shared Galois-theoretic structure can be handled by case analysis, suggesting an approach for unifying multiple unsolvable quintic witnesses (e.g., $x^5 - 4x + 2$ and $x^5 - 5x^4 + 10x^3 - 10x^2 + 25x - 5$ from `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01` and `inverse-galois-oq-06`) under a single `UnsolvableQuinticData` structure

references.note: Standard graduate algebra reference covering Galois theory in Chapters VI–VIII. Lang's treatment proves the Galois correspondence, develops solvability via the derived series, and presents Abel-Ruffini in the context of the broader theory of radical extensions and Kummer theory. Chapter VI Theorem 7.2 establishes the bidirectional Galois criterion ($\alpha$ solvable by radicals $\iff \text{Gal}(\text{minpoly}_F(\alpha))$ solvable, in characteristic 0 with sufficiently many roots of unity) which `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` uses contrapositively. Together with Dummit-Foote, this is the canonical graduate-level companion to the Lean formalization

references.title: A Machine-Checked Proof of the Odd Order Theorem
references.venue: Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP 2013), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 7998, pp. 163–179, Springer
references.note: The complete Coq formalization of the Feit-Thompson Odd Order Theorem (every finite group of odd order is solvable) — cited in the historical implications. At approximately 170,000 lines of Coq proof, this was the largest formalized mathematical result at the time and demonstrated the feasibility of machine-checking deep finite group theory. Since Feit-Thompson is the deepest known generalization of the solvability concept central to Abel-Ruffini (implying that any polynomial with odd-order Galois group is solvable by radicals), this formalization sits at the intersection of formal verification and the themes of this gallery entry

references.title: The Determination of Galois Groups
references.venue: Mathematics of Computation, vol. 27, no. 124, pp. 981–996
references.note: The classical algorithm for computing the Galois group of a polynomial over ℚ by resolvent factorization. Given $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $n$, Stauduhar's method identifies $\text{Gal}(f)$ as a subgroup of $S_n$ by successively checking which resolvent polynomials factor over ℚ. This is the practical complement to Abel-Ruffini's abstract impossibility: the theorem says non-solvable Galois group implies no radical formula; Stauduhar's algorithm (and its descendants in PARI/GP, Magma, SageMath) determines which Galois group a given polynomial has, making the unsolvability concrete and computable

references.title: A Database for Number Fields
references.venue: Mathematische Annalen 327: 715–742; database at http://galoisdb.math.upb.de/ and the LMFDB (https://www.lmfdb.org/NumberField/)
references.note: The Klüners-Malle Galois group database catalogs number-field extensions $K/\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $\leq 23$ alongside their Galois groups, discriminants, and class numbers. Combined with the LMFDB collaborative project (started 2007), it provides the modern computational counterpart to Abel-Ruffini: where this entry's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` says non-solvable Galois group implies no radical formula, the Klüners-Malle / LMFDB resources tabulate which Galois groups actually arise for which polynomials, turning the qualitative impossibility into quantitative statistics. Referenced in the LMFDB key insight.

references.title: Über die Beziehungen zwischen den Primidealen eines algebraischen Körpers und den Substitutionen seiner Gruppe
references.venue: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin, pp. 689–703
references.note: Frobenius's foundational theorem connecting prime factorization to Galois group structure: for an irreducible $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and an unramified prime $p$, the cycle type of the Frobenius element $\text{Frob}_p \in \text{Gal}(f)$ matches the degrees of the irreducible factors of $f \bmod p$. This is the original 'density theorem' restricted to cycle types corresponding to conjugacy classes — strictly weaker than Chebotarev's later sharpening but elementary enough that it could plausibly be formalized in Lean before the full Chebotarev theorem. The cornerstone of computational Galois theory. Referenced in keyInsights #13.

references.title: Determination of the density of the set of prime numbers, belonging to a given substitution class
references.venue: Izvestiya Rossiiskoi Akademii Nauk. Seriya Matematicheskaya (Russian); Mathematische Annalen 95: 191–228 (1925, German translation)
references.note: Chebotarev's density theorem: the natural density of unramified primes $p$ for which $\text{Frob}_p$ lies in a given conjugacy class $C \subseteq \text{Gal}(f)$ equals $|C|/|\text{Gal}(f)|$. The full quantitative refinement of Frobenius (1880). Together with Stauduhar's algorithm (1973), this is the engine that turns Abel-Ruffini's abstract impossibility into an effective procedure: factorize $f$ modulo a few hundred primes, count cycle types, match against the cycle-index polynomials of transitive subgroups of $S_n$ to identify $\text{Gal}(f)$. Cited in keyInsights #13 and the openQuestion on Chebotarev formalization.

references.authors: Lagarias, Jeffrey C. and Odlyzko, Andrew M.
references.title: Effective versions of the Chebotarev density theorem
references.venue: in *Algebraic Number Fields ($L$-functions and Galois Properties)* (A. Fröhlich, ed.), Academic Press, pp. 409–464
references.note: Effective Chebotarev: explicit error bounds for the density of primes with given Frobenius cycle type, conditional on GRH (and unconditional with weaker bounds). For a Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $n$ and discriminant $\Delta$, the smallest prime $p$ with $\text{Frob}_p$ in any nonempty conjugacy class is $O(\log^2 |\Delta|)$ under GRH. Practical Galois group computation algorithms (PARI/GP, Magma) implement effective Chebotarev: bounded-time verification of $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$ via a finite list of primes. Cited in the openQuestion on Chebotarev formalization.

references.title: On the irreducibility of certain trinomials
references.venue: Mathematica Scandinavica, vol. 4, pp. 287–302
references.note: Selmer's theorem: the trinomial $x^n - x - 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ for every $n \geq 2$. This irreducibility is the load-bearing first ingredient in the canonical Abel-Ruffini concrete witness $x^5 - x - 1$ that this entry's keyInsights and openQuestions repeatedly invoke. With Selmer's irreducibility in hand, the Galois group computation $\text{Gal}(x^5 - x - 1/\mathbb{Q}) \cong S_5$ proceeds via the standard textbook recipe (Dummit-Foote, Rotman): reduction modulo 2 supplies a 5-cycle in $\text{Gal}$ via Frobenius, the discriminant $\Delta = 2869 = 19 \cdot 151$ is not a perfect square (so $\text{Gal} \not\subseteq A_5$), and exactly three real plus two complex-conjugate roots contribute a transposition via complex conjugation — forcing $\text{Gal} = S_5$ since any transitive subgroup of $S_p$ for prime $p$ containing a $p$-cycle and a transposition is all of $S_p$. The Lean formalization of $x^5 - 4x + 2$ in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01` follows this blueprint via Eisenstein at $p = 2$ instead of Selmer's specialized trinomial irreducibility; a Selmer-style formalization establishing irreducibility of the entire family $x^n - x - 1$ in Mathlib remains an open challenge.
